title: Speed camera expansion limited pending provincial legislation
subtitle: Also: 2025 reserve fund update, brownfields program changes, Bill 17 effects on growth funding, and budget timeline.
overview: The Administration and Finance Committee spent most of its meeting on automated speed enforcement. Responding to the Province's stated plan to ban speed cameras, the committee recommended keeping the current program running and holding off on further expansion until the legislation is clear. It changed the motion so that the six cameras already installed and ready to go live can proceed. The committee also rejected a proposal to limit ticketing to school hours {{vote:m2}}. These are recommendations that Regional Council still has to adopt.

Staff also presented the 2025 Reserve Fund Update. The Region holds 79 reserve funds, but contingency savings sit below the recommended range and there is an ongoing shortfall in funding for renewing existing assets. Staff said Bill 17 delays development charge collection, and they are reprofiling growth projects in response. The Region can no longer take new brownfields applications because that role now rests with area municipalities. The first 2026 budget meeting is October 22.
Under other business, a councillor asked staff to report on ticket delivery during the Canada Post strike, and staff agreed to do so.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended, as amended, that the Region keep the current speed camera program running while it waits for details of the Province's pending legislation {{vote:m1}}.

decisions.item: Six ready cameras and expansion pause
decisions.detail: The committee amended the motion so that further previously planned expansion is halted at 28 school zones, allowing the six ready cameras to go live {{vote:m3}}.
The committee defeated an amendment to limit speed camera tickets to school operating hours and fine only vehicles well over the limit {{vote:m2}}.

debate: Supporters of the motion said it gave stability to the community and staff while the Province's plans are unclear, and avoided spending that might be wasted if cameras are banned. Some called it a middle-of-the-road approach.
A delegate from a provincial traffic organization urged the committee to keep the program, citing safety benefits in school zones and the higher chance of pedestrian survival at lower speeds.

On the school-hours amendment, supporters said it would respond to public complaints about tickets issued when no children are around. Opponents said it would confuse drivers and set two standards, and that speeding is a risk at all hours. They noted schools host evening activities.

One councillor opposed the main motion as premature, saying it sends the wrong message and that the ready cameras, including some in Cambridge, should go live. Others pointed to minimal added costs and the fact that the cameras were already paid for.

Several councillors said revenue is reinvested in road safety and that ending the program would shift costs to general taxpayers or police budgets. Others said the Region should be more open about how the program runs and should not treat fines as general revenue.
